title: Redwood technical deep dive - OOMs, timeouts, CUDA retry semantics (VPC/on-prem)
summary: Deep dive on recent OOMs/timeouts seen in Aurora's private deployment. Discussed kernel failures, kv cache eviction patterns, batching strategy, quantization tradeoffs, and retry semantics. Agreed next steps: gather logs (dmesg, CUDA logs), run controlled repro with p95 sequences, Redwood to share debug flags and a lightweight benchmark script, schedule pilot for dedicated pool evaluation.
next_steps: Aurora to share kube node and container logs + example request ids by 2026-07-20
Redwood SE (Mateo) to provide debug flags and a benchmark script by 2026-07-17
Schedule hands-on pilot to repro OOMs in Redwood Dedicated by 2026-07-27
action_items: Marcus Ng: collect /var/log/messages, dmesg, and container stdout for the two OOM incidents - due 2026-07-20
Mateo Ruiz: supply Redwood debug env vars, a repro harness, and suggested batch configs - due 2026-07-17
Priya Shah: enable verbose GC/allocator logs on Redwood instance and share instructions - due 2026-07-18
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Lina Park (Redwood AE), Mateo Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood SRE), Ethan Cole (Redwood Support), Samir Patel (Aurora CTO), Jenna Lowe (Aurora ML Platforms), Marcus Ng (Aurora Infra), Olga Roman (Aurora Security)

[00:00] Lina: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll kick us off. We set aside an hour to dig into the OOMs and timeouts you've been seeing on the private deployment, and go through retry semantics and the CUDA-related errors. Mateo and Priya from our infra team are here to go deeper.
[00:12] Samir: Appreciate it. We've been seeing intermittent OOM kills and occasionally long tail timeouts that block our API - traffic isn't huge but p95 latency spikes. We're worried it's either KV cache pressure or some CUDA kernel failure causing GPU memory fragmentation.
[00:26] Mateo: Got it. Do you have the approximate timestamps and any container logs? Even approximate request ids help.
[00:33] Jenna: Yeah I put a note in the calendar invite with two incidents - 2026-07-08 03:14 UTC and 2026-07-12 10:49 UTC, request ids winter-998 and winter-1023, sorry the transcription id is our internal. We can share the logs after the call.
[00:50] Priya: Quick question, are you running Redwood Private fully on-prem or a VPC-hosted deployment? Any GPUs with different driver versions across nodes?
[00:58] Marcus: It's a VPC deployment into our managed cluster. GPUs are a mixed fleet right now, a few A100s on one node pool and older V100s on another; drivers are slightly different, some nodes at 525.x, others at 470.x. We're in the middle of standardizing.
[01:14] Ethan: Mixed driver+hardware often shows up in weird kernel selection issues, yes. We usually recommend uniform driver stacks but we can also add kernel selection guards in the runtime.
[01:24] Samir: Also for context we enabled quantization for cost reasons (4-bit), and we've got a fairly aggressive batching policy to keep tokens/sec costs down. Might that increase memory pressure?
[01:36] Mateo: 4-bit quantization reduces model weights but can increase ephemeral workspace usage during kernel execution depending on the quantization codepath and fused kernels. Batching increases simultaneity and KV cache retention - those together can push peak GPU memory up.
[01:52] Jenna: We also saw some CUDA Error 700 reports in container logs - which I think maps to launch failures? The app logs say "CUDA_ERROR_LAUNCH_OUT_OF_RESOURCES".
[02:03] Priya: CUDA 700 is often insufficient resources for kernel launch — it can be due to block/grid sizes or the driver reporting fragmentation. Did you see any dmesg OOM-killer entries?
[02:13] Marcus: Two OOM-killer messages appear near the timestamps, one referencing a process named redwoooed (probably mis-typed) - it's messy, we'll pull the exact dmesg lines.
[02:23] Lina: Don't worry about typos, we've seen process names mangled in logs before. The important part is the sequence: kernel error, then a container restart, then timeouts upstream.
[02:32] Mateo: For retry semantics, how are you currently doing retries at the customer layer? Exponential backoff? Single retry?
[02:39] Samir: In our gateway we do two retries with a fixed 500ms backoff. For streaming calls we don't retry automatically because partial responses matter.
[02:47] Priya: That can cause duplicate work and additional memory spikes if retries overlap. Our runtime supports idempotent request ids and a dedupe layer to avoid double execution on transient errors, but it needs to be enabled and the client needs to pass idempotency keys.
[02:59] Jenna: We didn't enable dedupe initially, good point.
[03:03] Mateo: Also worth checking the timeout windows - if your gateway times out and retries quickly while the runtime is still unwinding a GPU alloc it can exacerbate fragmentation. We recommend a slightly longer client timeout for heavy seq lengths, or configure the runtime to return early failure with a short-circuit when memory pressure is high.
[03:19] Samir: Any debug flags we should flip to capture more info when the OOM occurs?
[03:24] Priya: Yes, we'll share a set of debug env vars. Key ones: REDWOOD_DEBUG_ALLOC_STATS, REDWOOD_CUDA_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG, and enable per-request KV cache tracing. That will add overhead but for repro it's useful.
[03:37] Marcus: If we enable alloc stats will that change timing and hide the bug?
[03:42] Mateo: It can, slightly. That's why we also recommend running a controlled repro harness that replays requests at a realistic cadence so we don't alter behavior too much. We'll provide a harness.
[03:51] Jenna: About KV cache, we've seen the cache holding a lot of prefixes for sessions that never complete. Do you evict LRU or time-based?
[03:59] Ethan: We use an adaptive eviction policy that weights recency and token footprint; but in private deployments default thresholds might be higher. If you have long session churn with small batches it can bloat. We can tune per-tenant cache caps.
[04:11] Samir: Could that eviction, when triggered, cause transient stalls and then timeouts?
[04:15] Priya: Eviction itself is fast, but if eviction plus immediate rehydration occurs because clients immediately reissue requests, that can spike allocations. Also if eviction frees CPU memory first and later GPU copy happens concurrently it might create allocation races.
[04:30] Mateo: For CUDA kernel failures, a common cause is mismatch of compiled kernels and driver ABI. If you have mixed driver versions you can hit a kernel that expects features not present. We saw similar artifacts when nodes had older cuda-runtime.
[04:43] Marcus: So standardizing drivers is high priority. Short term, is there a mitigation?
[04:48] Lina: Yes, we can pin runtime to conservative kernels and enable a fallback slower path that uses more generic kernels when driver capability detection fails. That trades latency for stability.
[04:58] Jenna: That seems reasonable for now, especially for VPC. For on-prem we might prefer a stable dedicated pool.
[05:04] Mateo: Another point: fragmentation. CUDA allocations can fragment if many allocations/frees of varying sizes happen. We have a tunable allocator that prefers pooling vs immediate free; switching to pooling reduces fragmentation at cost of memory footprint.
[05:18] Samir: So pooling could actually worsen peak memory?
[05:21] Mateo: It depends: pooling holds onto memory rather than returning to OS, which reduces failed allocs due to fragmentation, but it can raise held memory. For your workload with spikes, pooling can reduce OOMs even if reported usage is higher, because the allocator can satisfy new allocations from pooled chunks.
[05:36] Olga: From a security/compliance angle, if we retain more memory and caches we need to ensure sensitive context is cleared. Are there guarantees around zeroing KV cache evicted entries?
[05:46] Priya: Yes, we have a secure-erase flag that will overwrite GPU buffers on eviction; it's slower but meets compliance. We'll include the docs.
[05:54] Jenna: Back to retry semantics, can Redwood runtime expose an API status that indicates transient vs fatal errors so our gateway can make smarter decisions?
[06:02] Ethan: We do emit structured error codes: transient (E_TEMP_GPU/RESOURCE), driver/fatal (E_DRIVER_FAULT), and user-level (E_INPUT). We'll share the mapping. Using those codes your gateway can avoid retries on certain fatal classes.
[06:15] Marcus: Great. For the two incidents, what telemetry should we focus on sending you so you can correlate?
[06:21] Mateo: Container stdout/stderr, dmesg, nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps at the time, profiler traces (nsys) if possible, and our request ids and full request payloads. If you can attach small sanitized prompts that repro the long sequences that's ideal.
[06:35] Jenna: We can share sanitized payloads. Any guidance on sequence lengths to stress? We saw p95 token length was ~1k tokens.
[06:44] Mateo: 1k is fine. Also send a p99 set if possible. Include batching patterns (batch sizes and inter-request spacing).
[06:52] Samir: Do you recommend changing batch settings now?
[06:56] Lina: For a quick mitigation, reduce max batch size and increase batch timeout slightly to spread memory usage. Also set per-worker kv cache cap so one tenant can't blow through. We'll provide suggested values.
[07:08] Jenna: On quantization, do we need to disable 4-bit for now? We've seen the OOMs coincide with when we flipped quant.
[07:15] Mateo: Not necessarily. We should check if the 4-bit codepath on your driver/kernel combination spawns bigger temporary tensors during attention or dequant steps. If so, there's a short-term option: run 8-bit per-layer fallback for certain kernels, or enable a quantization-safe kernel set. We'll test with your logs.
[07:31] Marcus: Any specific CUDA errors we should hunt for beyond 700?
[07:35] Priya: Yes, look for 701 (operation timeout), 719 (illegal instruction), and any NCCL timeouts if you have multi-GPU. Also check for driver reinstatement messages in dmesg.
[07:46] Samir: We have some NCCL warnings from earlier when autoscaling happened. Might be related.
[07:51] Ethan: Autoscaling can cause node churn and partial NCCL groups; we recommend graceful draining and not killing GPU daemons mid-ops. We'll share a recommended node-drain script.
[08:01] Jenna: For the golden path, what's Redwood's recommended production config for VPC deployments with mixed GPUs?
[08:09] Mateo: Ideally homogeneous GPU and driver versions. If mixed is unavoidable: separate node pools per generation, use affinity so large models land on A100s, set conservative batch caps for older GPUs, and enable kernel fallback guards. Also use per-tenant dedicated pools for critical workloads.
[08:25] Samir: Could Dedicated help? If we moved to Redwood Dedicated instead of private VPC nodes, would that avoid these issues?
[08:33] Lina: Dedicated gives you a segregated GPU pool managed by Redwood with homogenous hardware and tuned driver stacks, plus SLA for latency. It reduces your maintenance burden but is a different procurement path. For an immediate stability fix, we can run a pilot on a small Dedicated pool.
[08:48] Marcus: Cost aside, a pilot would help repro and confirm fixes.
[08:51] Jenna: Agree.
[08:54] Priya: One more low-level note: enable REDWOOD_FORCE_FREE_ON_EVICT for a short window. It forces a release of GPU memory back to the allocator on eviction rather than pool hold - that can reduce held footprint but may increase fragmentation risk. Good for one-off cleanup.
[09:10] Mateo: We'll prepare a short doc: recommended debug flags, a repro harness, and suggested config changes (batch caps, kv cache caps, allocator mode). We'll include expected tradeoffs and commands to run nsys snapshots.
[09:22] Samir: Perfect. Who will be the point on Redwood side to coordinate the pilot?
[09:26] Lina: Mateo will lead the technical coordination, Priya will help on SRE/runbook items, and I'll handle contract/next-step coordination.
[09:33] Jenna: We'll start collecting logs and sign an NDA addendum if needed for deeper traces.
[09:39] Olga: We'll need the compliance doc for the secure erase behavior and the audit log retention policy - can you attach those?
[09:45] Lina: Yes, we'll attach security pack and the secure-erase docs.
[09:49] Samir: Any quick wins we can do right now to reduce p95 spikes?
[09:53] Mateo: Reduce max batch size to 50% of current, set batch timeout from 50ms to 80ms, set kv cache per-worker cap to 60% of default, and disable aggressive quantization per certain kernels. We'll provide exact commands.
[10:08] Jenna: Good. We'll try the config flips in a canary pool and report back.
[10:12] Lina: Nice, let's recap next steps.
[10:15] (recap) Lina: Aurora will gather logs and sanitized request payloads by 2026-07-20. Mateo will send debug flags and a repro harness by 2026-07-17. Redwood will prepare a pilot proposal for a small Dedicated pool by 2026-07-27. Security docs will be attached by Lina.
[10:34] Samir: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[10:37] Jenna: Thanks, talk soon.
